name: Center for Effective Philanthropy on AI in Nonprofits and Philanthropy
title: Center for Effective Philanthropy on AI in Nonprofits and Philanthropy
answer: CEP's AI pages collect blog guidance and survey findings on how foundations and nonprofits use AI. The most useful single finding comes from CEP's 'AI With Purpose' report: nearly 90 percent of nonprofits want to expand AI use, while 90 percent of foundations say they provide no support for AI implementation. The site also offers funder guidance on evaluating AI risk, quality, and efficacy, plus equity principles from the Kapor Foundation. It is a practical starting point for understanding the sector's AI supply-demand gap.

sections.body: CEP, the Center for Effective Philanthropy, publishes cep.org, a philanthropy research and commentary site. The AI-related pages reviewed are blog posts offering guidance to funders and foundations, plus citations to CEP's report 'AI With Purpose'. They cover AI equity, responsible AI principles, funder evaluation of AI projects, and strategic AI use. The reviewed text does not give individual post dates, though it cites events from December 2020 through March 2023 and refers to a recent CEP report.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Sarah Di Troia argues that philanthropy should help drive equity in AI and outlines four ways grantmakers can shape equitable AI tools and services. She notes that Google fired Timnit Gebru in December 2020 and later let go two other leading AI researchers, that Twitter laid off all but one member of its Machine Learning, Ethics, Transparency, and Accountability division in November 2022, that Microsoft eliminated its Ethics and Society team in January 2023, and that Twitch laid off or reassigned its Responsible AI group in March 2023. She says AI can bring huge benefits but also replicate bias and cement inequities, and she notes weak financial incentives in ESG and impact reporting and no federal AI regulation. She says funders should learn about AI, align administrative AI spending with equity values, and ask vendors about training data, bias testing, transparency, and monitoring. Allison Scott presents the Kapor Foundation's responsible AI principles, citing CEP's finding that only 10 percent of foundations support grantees on AI implementation and that 85 percent of nonprofits are not engaging in equitable AI. Jared Chung explains why funders freeze on AI evaluation, citing CEP's finding that nearly 90 percent of nonprofits want to expand AI use while 90 percent of foundations provide no support. He describes CareerVillage.org's 183 custom evaluation indicators and argues that risk management should focus on detection and remediation. Another post says CEP's report found 78 percent of foundations and 63 percent of nonprofits use AI for internal productivity, with similarly high rates for communication.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: CEP's pages give several figures. Di Troia cites Google's December 2020 dismissal of Timnit Gebru, two later departures of leading AI researchers, Twitter's November 2022 layoff of all but one member of its Machine Learning, Ethics, Transparency, and Accountability division, Microsoft's January 2023 elimination of its Ethics and Society team, and Twitch's March 2023 layoff or reassignment of its Responsible AI group. Scott cites $325B in big tech AI infrastructure investment this year, $149B in venture capital for AI startups, and hundreds of millions of dollars spent lobbying against AI regulation. She also cites CEP's finding that 10 percent of foundations support grantees on AI implementation, with half of that number focused on ethical AI, and that 85 percent of nonprofits are not engaging in equitable AI. She describes HumanityAI as a $500M, five-year initiative. Chung cites CEP's finding that nearly 90 percent of nonprofits are interested in expanding AI use and that 90 percent of foundations provide no support, with 10 percent funding AI projects, sometimes unintentionally through general operating support. He says CareerVillage.org developed 183 custom evaluation indicators. Another post cites CEP's finding that 78 percent of foundations and 63 percent of nonprofits use AI for internal productivity, with similarly high rates for communication, and describes a 26-section contract review that became a 10-plus hour project.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in nonprofits, CEP's pages are useful because they combine sector survey data with funder-facing guidance. The data show strong nonprofit interest in AI alongside weak foundation support, which helps explain the supply-demand gap. The guidance gives practical questions funders can ask about training data, bias testing, transparency, monitoring, evaluation methods, and accountability systems. The Kapor Foundation principles add a framework for judging whether AI projects are equitable and prosocial. The CareerVillage and Tarjimly examples show how nonprofits can measure AI quality and efficacy without changing their core mission metrics. The pages are therefore a source for understanding both the state of AI adoption in philanthropy and the terms on which funders may support it.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The reviewed pages are blog posts and report citations rather than a comprehensive technical manual. They focus on foundations and funders, with nonprofit examples, and do not cover every nonprofit subfield or provide detailed implementation instructions. Several posts are advocacy and guidance, arguing for equity and responsible AI rather than presenting neutral technical assessments. The text does not give individual post dates, though it cites events from 2020 to 2023 and refers to a recent CEP report. It also does not provide a full methodology for the survey findings it cites.
